headline: Two Bizarre New Sea Spiders Discovered in Canadian Waters
meta_description: Scientists at UBC identified two previously unknown sea spider species in the Salish Sea, the first new species documented there in nearly 100 years.
summary_short: Researchers discovered two strange new sea spider species in the Salish Sea near Vancouver, including one with hairy legs and red eyes that grooms itself with comb-like…
body:
Scientists at the University of British Columbia have identified two previously unknown sea spider species living in the Salish Sea, marking the first new species formally described from the region in nearly 100 years. One species, named Callipallene pilosuspedes for its distinctive hairy legs, sports striking red eyes and a triangular mouth rimmed with sensory tendrils. Researchers observed this creature using comb-like spines on its appendages to groom and clean its own body—a behavior rarely documented in sea spiders. The second species, Tanystylum kiixin, named after an ancient Indigenous village site near where it was collected, frequently appears covered in tiny parasites and debris, creating what lead researcher Cormac Toler-Scott describes as "an ecosystem within an ecosystem within an ecosystem." The discoveries, published in Organisms Diversity & Evolution, combine detailed physical observations with genetic analysis to illuminate the hidden diversity of these ancient marine animals.

Toler-Scott conducted the research during his master's degree in zoology, collecting specimens between September 2023 and August 2024 from depths reaching 18 meters around Quadra Island, Vancouver, Bamfield, and Victoria. He began the work because so little was known about sea spiders in the region—a knowledge gap that makes it impossible to understand how climate change and human disturbance affect these marine invertebrates. Sea spiders belong to a lineage stretching back roughly 500 million years and possess bizarre biology: they breathe through their skin, males carry and raise the young, and females develop eggs inside their limbs before releasing them through dedicated pores.

While only a single specimen of the hairy-legged species was found, Toler-Scott emphasizes that the Salish Sea likely harbors additional undocumented sea spider species waiting to be discovered. The team has produced an identification guide to help scientists distinguish sea spider species throughout the region, and both newly discovered species have been registered in a global database.
quick_facts: First new sea spider species from Salish Sea documented in nearly 100 years
Callipallene pilosuspedes has red eyes and uses combs to groom itself
Collected from depths up to 18 meters near Vancouver, Bamfield, and Victoria
Sea spiders are 500 million years old and breathe directly through their skin
Male sea spiders carry and raise eggs on their own bodies
